title: Why Jesus Is Called the Lamb of God
paragraphs: Why Jesus Is Called the Lamb of God
At first glance, the title sounds gentle.
Almost fragile.
Of all the names that could describe the Savior of the world — King, Deliverer, Conqueror, Judge — Scripture repeatedly calls Jesus something unexpected:
“The Lamb of God.”
When John the Baptist first saw Jesus approaching the Jordan River, he did not introduce Him as a teacher, prophet, or miracle worker.
He made a declaration that would echo through history:

“Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.”
— John 1:29
To modern readers, that phrase might sound poetic.
But to the people standing there that day, it was shocking.
Because for over a thousand years, lambs had been dying on Israel’s altars.
Every morning.
Every evening.
Every Passover.
Every time someone sinned.
A lamb was offered.
And every sacrifice carried the same message:

Sin has a cost.
And something innocent must pay it.
But those sacrifices were never meant to last forever.
They were signs.
Shadows.
Prophetic pictures pointing toward something — or Someone — greater.
The story really begins in the book of Exodus.
The night Israel was about to leave Egypt, God gave a very specific instruction.
Every household was to take a spotless lamb, sacrifice it, and place its blood on the doorposts of their home.
That night, judgment passed through the land.
But when the Lord saw the blood, He said:
“I will pass over you.”
A lamb died…
So the people could live.
Centuries later, during another Passover season, Jesus would be crucified in Jerusalem.
Not randomly.
Not accidentally.
But perfectly timed in God’s redemptive plan.
The lambs being sacrificed in the temple that day were symbols.
Jesus was the reality.
But the symbolism goes even deeper.
In the Old Testament sacrificial system described in Leviticus, a person who sinned would bring an animal to the altar.
The animal was not guilty.
The person was.
Yet the animal died in their place.
This established one of the most powerful spiritual truths in Scripture:
Substitution.
The guilty live.
The innocent takes the cost.
Still, those sacrifices had a limitation.
They had to be repeated.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Because animal blood could symbolize forgiveness…
But it could not permanently remove sin.
That is why the prophet Isaiah wrote something extraordinary about the coming Messiah hundreds of years before Jesus was born.

“He was led like a lamb to the slaughter… and as a sheep before its shearers is silent, so He did not open His mouth.”
— Isaiah 53:7
The prophecy revealed something unexpected.
The Savior would not first conquer through force.
He would conquer through sacrifice.
When Jesus went to the cross, He was not simply dying as a martyr.
He was fulfilling thousands of years of prophecy, symbolism, and sacrificial imagery.
Every altar.
Every lamb.
Every offering.
Every drop of blood.
All of it was pointing to one moment in history.
The cross.
Unlike the sacrifices of the temple, Jesus did not need to die repeatedly.
Scripture makes this clear.
He offered Himself once for all.
The system of endless sacrifice ended because the perfect sacrifice had finally come.
That is why the Bible does not only call Him the Lamb who was slain.
It also describes heaven worshiping Him with these words:

“Worthy is the Lamb who was slain.”
— Revelation 5:12
Think about that for a moment.
In heaven, Jesus is still celebrated with that title.
Not just King.
Not just Lord.
The Lamb.
Because the cross will always be the center of the story of redemption.
Here is the stunning paradox of the Gospel:
The Lion of Judah saved the world…
by becoming a Lamb.
Power through sacrifice.
Victory through surrender.
Life through death.
And because the Lamb took our place, forgiveness is now possible for anyone who believes.
No more endless sacrifices.
No more altars filled with animals.
The final Lamb has already been given.
And the same Lamb who was slain…
is now seated on the throne.
That is the Gospel.
That is why Jesus is called the Lamb of God.
And that is why millions of believers across the world still declare today:
“Worthy is the Lamb.”
Reflection question:
When you hear Jesus called “the Lamb of God,” what part of that truth moves you the most — His sacrifice, His innocence, or His victory over sin and death?
